damage.damage_scenario: Requests are checked or stored wrongly, so certificates are issued for the wrong subject or with the wrong lifetime.

Operators and internal services cannot request or renew certificates for several days. Renewals lapse, services fail as their certificates expire, and on-call teams issue emergency certificates by hand, bypassing the normal approval checks.
A requester gets certificates approved that their role does not allow.
Certificates are signed that were never approved.
Approved certificates wait unsigned and issuing stops.
Request details and the names, emails and phone numbers of requesters are exposed outside the security team, including the business reason for each certificate, which reveals internal project names.
Records of who requested and approved certificates are changed.
Certificate history cannot be read, so audits and renewals stall.
Nobody can prove who approved a certificate.
Revoked certificates drop off the published list and are trusted again. A certificate revoked after a key leak can then impersonate an internal service until someone notices and revokes it again.
Relying services cannot fetch the list and either fail closed or skip the check.
Relying services accept a forged revocation list.

The signing key leaves the key store, and whoever holds it can issue certificates every relying service trusts. All issued certificates become suspect, the key must be replaced and every service reissued.
The key is replaced, so issued certificates no longer chain to the trusted root.
Certificates signed by another key are accepted as the portal’s own.
Sign-in tokens and request contents are read on the way in.
A request is changed in transit, so the certificate is issued for something else.

damage.damage_scenario: Requests are checked or stored wrongly, so certificates are issued for the wrong subject or with the wrong lifetime.

Operators and internal services cannot request or renew certificates for several days. Renewals lapse, services fail as their certificates expire, and on-call teams issue emergency certificates by hand, bypassing the normal approval checks.
A requester gets certificates approved that their role does not allow.
Certificates are signed that were never approved.
Request details and the names, emails and phone numbers of requesters are exposed outside the security team, including the business reason for each certificate, which reveals internal project names.
Nobody can prove who approved a certificate.
Revoked certificates drop off the published list and are trusted again. A certificate revoked after a key leak can then impersonate an internal service until someone notices and revokes it again.
Relying services cannot fetch the list and either fail closed or skip the check.
Relying services accept a forged revocation list.

The signing key leaves the key store, and whoever holds it can issue certificates every relying service trusts. All issued certificates become suspect, the key must be replaced and every service reissued.
The key is replaced, so issued certificates no longer chain to the trusted root.
Sign-in tokens and request contents are read on the way in.
A request is changed in transit, so the certificate is issued for something else.

04.text: Relying services check the revocation list on every connection, so a missing entry is used straight away.
Requesters are company staff, so their contact details count as personal data under the privacy policy.
There is no second signing key ready, so replacing a leaked key means reissuing every certificate.

05.text: The hop between the certificate service and the key service has no mutual TLS. The documents do not say either way.
TLS ends at the load balancer, so the hop to the gateway is in clear text.
The deploy identity can call the key store export function.

06.text: Physical access to the backup room is controlled by the data centre provider, so this risk can be accepted.
A shared admin login is still in use, so approvals cannot be traced to a person today.
The deploy identity can call the key store export function.

04.you: Legal feels high here. An over-approved certificate breaks our own approval policy, not a customer contract.
04.reply: Agreed. Nothing in the documents ties role approval to a customer contract; it is an internal policy breach, which is Moderate.

05.you: The log reader role has this access by default in the current setup, so it is not a special condition.
05.reply: Agreed. If the role is broad by default, nothing outside the attacker’s control has to line up, so complexity is Low.

06.you: The log reader role is being removed in the next release, and the records are already encrypted at rest. Can we accept this one?
06.reply: Yes, if the removal is tracked. With the role gone the attack path closes; I suggest Accept and noting the release as the reason.

differences: Attack feasibility: the designs draw four levels from fixed CVSS thresholds; the pipeline has five, calculated from the factors by the engine (very low to very high).
Risk score: the designs read 1 to 5 off a matrix; the pipeline multiplies the impact value (0 to 3) by the feasibility value (1 to 5), 0 to 15, with five levels (informational to critical).
Who is affected: free text in the designs, one of five parties in the pipeline.
Attack path: three or four steps in the designs, five in the pipeline; the sentences after the third are written for the fixture.
Treatment: the designs offer Reduce and Accept; the pipeline has Reduce, Accept, Share and Avoid, and only informational and low risks can be accepted.
04 shows 17 damage scenarios; four have no threat in the design, so the fixture gives each one a threat to make it rated.
